paras: The lynching of Andrew Grandstaff took place at Viroqua, Vernon County, Wisconsin, in the early morning of June 2, 1888, when a mob broke into the county jail, took Grandstaff from the sheriff and hanged him from an oak in front of the court house. Grandstaff had been arrested the night before on a charge of murdering Reuben Drake, Drake's wife and their two grandchildren, and officers said he had confessed. The wire story ran from Pennsylvania to Montana, and Wisconsin weeklies divided over it.

On May 25 a neighbor found Reuben Drake and his wife dead on the floor of their farmhouse in the town of Kickapoo, and two grandchildren, children of James Dupee, in bed with their throats cut. A coroner's jury found that the four had been murdered by unknown parties. Grandstaff, a hunter and lumberman in his twenties, had a 'hard' reputation in the Kickapoo Valley and had been shot at a school meeting at Kickapoo Center in February.

C. J. Farrell of Pinkerton's Chicago force, with former sheriffs Goodell and Morley, arrested Grandstaff on the night of May 31 and brought him to Viroqua the next morning. According to the dispatches, he confessed to the officers that he had killed the Drakes while trying to rob them, a confession later printed as signed and sworn before a justice of the peace. As talk of lynching spread through the day, the sheriff telegraphed Governor Rusk for help, but the Watertown Republican said the countryside sided with the mob and few deputies could be found.

Between 11 o'clock and midnight a crowd surrounded the jail and demanded the prisoner, and when the sheriff refused, the men broke in with axes and overpowered the officers. The Rock Island Argus wrote that deputies at first drove the mob back and that Grandstaff, armed with a club, held his cell door for more than an hour. He was brought out bound, covered with blood from wounds received as the steel cage was battered down.

At the jail entrance James Dupee asked him whether he had killed the children, and Grandstaff answered that he had not been there. The mob then hoisted him on the court-house oak and let him down to press for a confession. After the second hoisting he said that Frank and Elisha Carey had planned the murder, a statement the dispatches said was not believed. By the wire account he hung eleven minutes before he died, and his body was left on the tree until morning.

The Mineral Point Tribune reported at the end of June that no coroner's jury had been called on the lynching, so there would be no official record of it. No report of arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage, though one dispatch said 'many leading citizens' had been prominent in the hanging.

The Viroqua dispatch ran on June 2 in papers as far apart as Indianapolis, Lancaster and Memphis. Headlines ran from 'Horrible Lynching' in Memphis to 'Lynched the Drake Butcher' in Rock Island, and most papers printed the confession beside the hanging, treating his denials as untrue. Into mid-June, one-sentence digests ran in Minnesota, Wisconsin and Vermont weeklies, most calling him 'a young desperado.'

Some Wisconsin accounts wrote from the mob's side: the Watertown Republican said the murderer 'found retribution on an improvised gallows,' and the Wood County Reporter said he 'came into the world a disgrace and has just gone out a disgrace.' The Mineral Point Tribune closed its note with 'One incarnate fiend has met his just desserts.' The Grant County Herald, by contrast, judged it only 'probable, but not absolutely certain' that the right man was hanged and called lynch law a 'very dangerous' precedent. From across the state line, the St. Paul Daily Globe remarked that with 'a first-class murder and a first-class lynching' Wisconsin was doing well 'in the advertising line.'

The wire reports put the mob at 1,000 men, while the Grant County Herald said about 100. Most dispatches said he died after the second hoisting, the Argus said the third, and a Connecticut summary said his 'executioners tortured him' for 30 minutes and placed the case at Richland Center.

accounts.label: Wire report (Viroqua, 2 a.m.)
accounts.gist: A thousand men broke into the jail, battered down the steel cage, hanged Grandstaff from a tree, let him down twice, and he hung eleven minutes; his claim of innocence and his naming of the Careys were 'not thought to be true'.

accounts.label: Rock Island Argus (Viroqua, June 4)
accounts.gist: The sheriff and a dozen deputies at first repulsed the mob; Grandstaff held his cell with a club for over an hour, denied killing the children to their father, and was strangled on the third hoisting.

accounts.label: Grant County Herald
accounts.gist: About 100 men came at 11:50 p.m.; a second confession was 'extorted'; his last words implicated two neighbors and were not believed.

accounts.label: Watertown Republican
accounts.gist: The governor told the sheriff to swear in deputies until militia came; the countryside sympathized with the mob, and the authorities kept the confession quiet to hold the mob back.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Viroqua wire under headlines such as 'Murderer Lynched', 'Horrible Lynching' and 'Lynched the Drake Butcher', with the confession printed beside it.

The Watertown Republican wrote that the murderer 'found retribution' and that 'Judge Lynch ruled supreme'; the Wood County Reporter said he 'came into the world a disgrace and has just gone out a disgrace'.
The Grant County Herald said the right man was probably but not certainly hanged and called lynch law a 'very dangerous' precedent.
The Mineral Point Tribune ended its note: 'One incarnate fiend has met his just desserts.'
The St. Paul Daily Globe joked that with 'a first-class murder and a first-class lynching' Wisconsin was doing well 'in the advertising line'.

conflicts.note: The 1,000 figure is the wire's; the Grant County Herald is a Wisconsin weekly writing a week later.

versions.value: died after the second hoisting; hung eleven minutes

conflicts.note: A15 itself repeats the eleven-minute figure alongside the third hoisting.
The May 25 La Crosse report says shots were heard at 11 o'clock the previous night (A1), which fits May 24.
Only the Willimantic news summary names Richland Center; A11 shows a Richland Center dateline on an arrest dispatch, the likely source of the error.
